title: The Library of Missing Datasets
summary: In 2016, artist and researcher Mimi Ọnụọha created The Library of Missing Datasets, an installation consisting of a filing cabinet filled with labelled but empty folders. Each folder represented information that might reasonably be expected to exist, but was absent from otherwise data-rich systems. Examples included information about people excluded from public housing because of criminal records and the mobility of older adults with disabilities. By giving these absences a physical form, Ọnụọha drew attention to the social, political and institutional decisions that determine what gets recorded. Her accompanying research explored why datasets remain missing, including lack of incentives to collect them, difficulties in measurement, and situations where the absence of data benefits particular groups.
thoughts: As we become more reliant on genAI to give us the answers it's important to have artists like Mimi Ọnụọha to help us engage critically with what it can't tell us.
discovery:
We often think of missing data as a problem to be solved. If only we could collect more information, we might make better decisions. But Mimi Ọnụọha's Library of Missing Datasets suggests that the gaps themselves can tell us something important.

Data doesn't simply exist, waiting to be collected. Someone has to decide what is worth measuring, invest in collecting it, and determine how it will be categorised. What remains unmeasured can reveal whose experiences are overlooked, which questions institutions prioritise, and where power lies.

Yet there's an interesting tension. Missing data can make people invisible to decision-makers, but collecting information about them can also expose them to surveillance, discrimination or harm.

Perhaps the challenge isn't simply to fill the gaps in our datasets. It's to ask who decided what should be measured, whose interests those decisions serve, and whether more information will necessarily lead to better outcomes.

reflections.name: Tesse
reflections.text:
When I tried to open the link, I actually couldn't find the library. A
little google search brought me here:
https://mimi-onuoha-9s0o.squarespace.com/the-library-of-missing-datasets
and https://github.com/MimiOnuoha/missing-datasets - what a treat to get
this piece in my inbox!

reflections.name: Erin
reflections.text: What a lovely project! I wonder if it inspired any changes.

title: Mapping a city by its smells
summary: In April 2013, artist and researcher Kate McLean invited 44 people to explore Amsterdam using their noses rather than their eyes. Across ten guided smellwalks, participants recorded more than 650 encounters with different smells, describing their intensity, location and personal associations. McLean organised these observations into 50 categories and created a colourful map showing where smells originated, how far they might travel and how prevailing winds influenced their movement. The resulting Smellmap: Amsterdam, exhibited in 2014, included specially recreated scents that visitors could experience alongside the map. The project demonstrated a method for documenting an aspect of urban environments that conventional maps rarely represent: their changing sensory character.
thoughts: As a geographer by training this a reminder of always reflecting on the subjectivity of maps - who chooses what gets mapped, and why did they make the choices they did? I like how this maps a city from a completely different perspective, and I wonder if the brief was different, like using hearing rather than smell, the map might look completely different. In a world of big data, it is another reminder that the maps we create end up being of the data we collected, and not the data we didn't. The things that are important to some people may not be visible.
discovery:
Most maps tell us where things are, but the Amsterdam Smellmap asks a different question: what does a place actually feel like to experience? By mapping smells, Kate McLean captured something that conventional geographic data often misses: the subjective, fleeting and deeply personal character of our surroundings.

What's particularly interesting is that the project didn't treat these subjective experiences as unreliable observations to be discarded. Instead, it brought them together to reveal patterns that no single participant could have identified alone.

This raises questions about what we consider legitimate evidence. Scientific measurements offer consistency and comparability, but they don't necessarily capture everything that matters to people. How might our understanding of a place change if we mapped not just its physical characteristics, but how people experience it?

Perhaps the most revealing maps are sometimes those that show us what we've never thought to measure.

reflections.name: Janot
reflections.text:
Reminds me of a fascinating Amsterdam science museum exhibit geared to draw 
teenagers: *on sex*! It displayed a bunch of stinky t-shirts that 
researchers had got a bunch of guys to wear for a few days. The experiment 
was for other people - generally on the other side of the sex spectrum - to 
see whether each smelled good, bad or indifferent - to find out if the more 
closely genetically related we are the more unpleasant we smell to each 
other! Being subtly more attracted to potential breeding partners who are 
more distantly related (given no human being is more than about 50th cousin 
to any other human) than our biologically close family is “nature’s” way of 
encouraging hybrid vigor! Turns out our sense of smell is wired for mixing 
up the gene pool…An evolutionary biology principle lurking in these depths? 
To borrow one of my father’s jokes: to keep the species from swimming into 
the shallow end of the gene pool!

reflections.name: Sayanti
reflections.text:
Oh wow, I wonder if they could smell the stroopwaffels from Amsterdam. I
would love to have been a part of this!

title: The rocket explained using only 1,000 words
summary: In November 2012, cartoonist Randall Munroe published an xkcd comic explaining NASA's Saturn V rocket using only the 1,000 most common English words. Because technical terms such as rocket were excluded, he renamed it the Up Goer Five, producing a detailed diagram with descriptions such as “people box” for the crew capsule. The comic inspired geneticist Theo Sanderson to create an online text editor that checks whether writing stays within the same restricted vocabulary. Scientists subsequently took up the challenge, producing descriptions of research ranging from particle physics to volcanology. The exercise became a popular science-communication activity, including at scientific conferences.
thoughts: How clearly are we explaining to people something that is maybe hard to understand? Is this now a dead art form because we have know-everything machines to do this for us? Sometimes I think that this is what I end up doing anyway when I try to speak in a different language!
discovery:
The Up Goer Five is funny because it turns sophisticated engineering into something that sounds almost childlike. But beneath the humour is a serious communication challenge: how much of our expertise depends on specialised language, and how much can we explain without it?

Technical vocabulary is useful because it allows experts to communicate complex ideas precisely and efficiently. But it can also create barriers, particularly when people from different disciplines need to work together. Restricting ourselves to everyday words forces us to reconsider what we actually mean, rather than relying on terminology that others may not understand.

There is a tension here, though. Simplifying language can make ideas more accessible, but it can also sacrifice important distinctions. Perhaps the real skill isn't explaining everything simply, but knowing which complexities matter, and which are merely habits of our own discipline.

reflections.name: Erin
reflections.text:
I'm a huge fan of Randall Monroe - he eventually wrote a whole book on
this. I've spent the last few days at a conference in which we argued over
the use of "forecast verification" vs "forecast benchmarking" lol. Munroe
shows that precision of language is both critical and irrelevant.

reflections.name: Sayanti
reflections.text:
Ah I wish we had something similar to communicate our climate work to
people from completely different fields. I often assume that by now
everyone knows what climate change is doing to us, but very now and then I
am shocked that I might be in a bubble.

title: One death is never just one death
summary: When we count the human cost of conflict, we usually focus on the number of people killed. But what about the people they leave behind? In a 2024 study published in Science Advances, researchers examined the wider consequences of conflict-related deaths across 16 populations, estimating how many surviving family members experience the loss of a parent, child, sibling or spouse. Their findings revealed how the impact of a single death extends far beyond the individual. In Syria, for example, each death was associated with an average of approximately 1.4 bereaved parents and 2.5 bereaved children. The researchers argued that conventional mortality statistics capture only part of the human cost of armed conflict. By quantifying bereavement, their work offers a different way of understanding the scale and lasting consequences of human loss.
thoughts: This feels like the counterpart to the Wind Phone from an academic perspective. I feel like the switch to 'number of people bereaved' changes the narrative. While this paper is from a conflict perspective, I think many aspects apply to fatalities from natural hazards. The loss of a caregiver or source of household incomes will have long-term impacts, and I think it has implications for disaster memory too.
image_credit: Graph: Max Planck Institute for Demographic Research; based on Alburez-Gutierrez et al. (2024), Science Advances.
discovery:
We often measure the human impact of disasters and conflicts through numbers: deaths, injuries, people displaced. These figures are important, but they can make the consequences seem more contained than they really are. Bereavement research reveals something that conventional statistics often overlook: a single death can profoundly affect many other lives.

This raises an interesting question about how we define and measure impact. If our indicators focus only on immediate outcomes, what longer-term consequences are we missing? The effects of bereavement can extend across generations, influencing families, communities and the support networks on which people depend.

There is also a challenge for communication. Numbers help us understand the scale of a crisis, but they can obscure the relationships behind them. Perhaps understanding human impact requires us to count not just individuals, but the connections between them.

reflections.name: Sayanti
reflections.text:
I tend to agree. Most losses are just counted in hard stats, and
psychosocial impacts of losses which can't be easily put into digits are
hardly captured. Also similar to disaster losses. There are almost always
more stories of traditional land lost, cultures disrupted. Which is why I
am really excited to see how the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage
starts performing and how countries are asking for compensation and whether
they even count these losses, as the Fund specifically seeks to fund
non-economic losses.

title: Why the same songs become hits in different worlds
summary: In 2006, researchers Matthew Salganik, Peter Dodds and Duncan Watts recruited 14,341 people to participate in an online music experiment called MusicLab. Participants listened to unfamiliar songs and could download those they liked. Some made their choices independently, while others could see what previous participants had downloaded. Crucially, the researchers divided the latter group into eight separate online worlds, each with the same songs but a different emerging popularity ranking. The results were striking. When people could see what others were choosing, the most popular songs became more popular and the least popular became less popular. But which particular songs became hits varied substantially between worlds. Even with the same music and broadly similar audiences, popularity proved surprisingly unpredictable. The experiment demonstrated how social influence can amplify small initial differences into very different collective outcomes.
thoughts: I can't help find this a little unsettling, that even in the relatively small confines of this experiment the 'culture' evolved so chaotically. What does that mean for everything we do?
image_credit: Photograph: Bruce Mars · CC0 1.0 · Wikimedia Commons
discovery:
The MusicLab experiment challenges a comforting assumption: that the most successful ideas are necessarily the best. Quality matters, but popularity is also shaped by chance, timing and the choices of others. Once something attracts attention, that attention can become a reason for further attention.

But there's another fascinating implication: the way we collect people's opinions may influence the diversity of ideas we hear. If someone reads several enthusiastic responses before writing their own, they might unconsciously follow the emerging consensus. This is why Daily Hummingbird contributors are invited to reflect independently before seeing what others think.

The same principle applies to scientific research, interdisciplinary workshops and group decision-making. Would a meeting produce different ideas if everyone contributed independently before the most senior person spoke?

Perhaps the challenge isn't simply helping good ideas spread, but creating the conditions for different ideas to emerge.

reflections.name: Erin
reflections.text:
This is a great reminder of the role of randomness in our lives. We
perceive that we are rational actors operating under certain decision
rules, but in reality, we are influenced by millions of factors
subconsciously. I would love to study why certain things go viral.

title: The scientific study that proved parachutes don't work
summary: In December 2018, researchers published a randomised controlled trial in The BMJ investigating whether parachutes prevent death or serious injury when jumping from aircraft. Twenty-three volunteers were randomly assigned either a parachute or an empty backpack before jumping. Remarkably, the researchers found no difference between the two groups: nobody was injured. There was, however, a rather important detail. All 23 participants had jumped from stationary aircraft on the ground, at an average height of just 60 centimetres. The researchers had been unable to recruit anyone willing to jump from a flying aircraft without a parachute. Published in the journal's Christmas edition, the deliberately humorous study demonstrated how a perfectly legitimate experimental design can produce a statistically sound but practically meaningless result when the participants and circumstances are unrepresentative.
thoughts: A reminder that the best way to call something out is with humour! Also, more seriously, to really deeply consider our experimental design, and what is being unintentionally excluded. For example, mortality data collected by a hospital is only representative of the people who had the capacity to get there in the first place.
discovery: The parachute trial is funny precisely because the science is technically sound. The researchers followed the principles of a randomised controlled trial, but the circumstances were so different from those in which parachutes are actually needed that the results were meaningless for the real-world question. It illustrates a fundamental distinction between internal validity and external validity: an experiment can reliably tell us what happened under the conditions studied, without telling us whether the findings apply elsewhere. This is particularly important when evidence is used to inform decisions in unfamiliar or extreme circumstances. We often ask whether research is rigorous, but perhaps we should spend just as much time asking whether it is relevant. The most statistically robust answer to the wrong question may be less useful than an imperfect answer to the right one.

reflections.name: Macarena
reflections.text:
Lol… this funny story highlights why we need to read the methods section!
More importantly, it’s why we need experts to translate science into
something useful for policymakers, educators and, crucially, communications
and newspapers!

reflections.name: Erin
reflections.text:
I adore this study!! I think we need to be more critical of our scientific
knowledge: how we select the questions we want to answer, how we answer
them, and how we communicate the results. I wonder if we could do a few
examples of this kind of silly thing with climate data analysis.

reflections.name: Janot
reflections.text:
Pedantry aside. These researchers were after the wrong accolade - their 
research method might fare better with the Darwin awards;)

title: The pigeons that became environmental reporters
summary: In 2006, artist and engineer Beatriz da Costa recruited an unlikely team of environmental investigators: homing pigeons. Working with students, engineers and pigeon enthusiasts in California, she developed PigeonBlog, equipping birds with miniature backpacks containing air-pollution sensors, GPS receivers and mobile-phone technology. As the pigeons flew, their equipment transmitted measurements of pollutants, including carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides, to an online map. The project combined experimental environmental monitoring with public art, making otherwise invisible pollution visible through an unexpected form of citizen science. Nearly two decades later, in October 2024, PigeonBlog was revived as part of an exhibition celebrating da Costa's work in Los Angeles.
thoughts: I really like this merging of art and science, as a scientist I'm wondering what the data was used for, but I bet someone with an art background would have a completely different take on it. This also seems similar to the fish doorbell; a way to capture the public's imagination to get people thinking about an environmental problem. I could see a classroom of kids being interested in where pigeons experienced the highest pollution levels!
image_credit: Photograph: HTO · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
discovery: PigeonBlog is a wonderful example of how art can change the relationship between science and the public. The pigeons were not necessarily the most accurate or efficient way to measure air pollution, but they made something invisible both visible and interesting. A conventional monitoring station produces data; a pigeon wearing a sensor backpack produces curiosity, conversation and perhaps a different kind of engagement with that data. There is an important tension here: scientific credibility depends on measurement quality, but public engagement often depends on imagination. Could an unconventional approach sometimes achieve more than a technically superior one, simply because people want to pay attention?

reflections.name: Sayanti
reflections.text:
In Germany, pigeons are called as the dirty flying rats of the sky. I guess
every animal is playing a role in the ecosystem, and we forget that too
often. And this experiment showed that these pigeons can help us too, going
beyond what they were meant to be doing. I wish this story was better known.

reflections.name: Janot
reflections.text: In Spanish, paloma still means both pigeon & dove, is lovely as a girl’s name, and still carries religious meaning. For thousands of years we humans domesticated the pigeon, built beautiful dovecotes to encourage their cohabitation, described their delicate flavour as squab, and trained them to serve us as a sort of avian internet, carrying messages to their intended recipients at astonishing distance. How did the pigeons who still co-inhabit our urban settlements become so maligned - rats with wings? Although the English-speaking world betrayed our once closely-allied & admired pigeons, clearly they continue to be willing collaborators, carrying little backpacks full of GHG pollution sensors. Perhaps the PigeonBlog is reviving a bit of inter-species reverence?

reflections.name: Macarena
reflections.text:
We have the tools, the knowledge and funds to defeat environmental
challenges.  We just have to care enough to put it all together and
collaborate to make it work.

title: Vision Zero
summary:
In 1995, shortly after becoming Sweden’s head of road safety, Claes Tingvall was confronted by a crash on the E4 motorway near Stockholm in which five young people were killed after their car left the road and struck the concrete base of a streetlight. As a 2024 BBC Future profile of Tingvall recounts, the crash helped crystallise a radically different way of thinking about road safety. Rather than asking only what the driver had done wrong, Tingvall asked why an ordinary mistake had been allowed to become fatal.

That thinking became the basis of Vision Zero, adopted by the Swedish Parliament in 1997. It accepts that people will sometimes speed, lose concentration or make bad decisions, so roads and vehicles should be designed to prevent those mistakes from killing them. One early experiment installed central wire barriers on a dangerous stretch of road despite fears they would cause more crashes. Tingvall’s response was essentially: that was the point — hitting a forgiving barrier was preferable to crossing into oncoming traffic. The approach helped shift responsibility for road deaths from individual road users alone towards the people who design and manage the transport system.
thoughts:
This is a fascinating profile of someone who has changed a mindset against a lot of pushback. I loved the example of how Tingvall had to persuade people to accept an increase in the number of crashes because it would bring down the number of fatalities.

I wonder how it might change our thinking around Early Warning Systems. Changing the target and mindset changes the interventions.
image_credit: Photograph: Lavas · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
discovery: Vision Zero reframes failure in a powerful way: the question is not simply whether people followed the rules, but whether the system was designed to tolerate predictable human error. That has implications far beyond road safety. In early warning, humanitarian action and climate-risk management, people will misunderstand, delay, improvise or make decisions under pressure. A resilient system should not depend on perfect behaviour; it should be designed so that ordinary mistakes do not cascade into catastrophe.

reflections.name: Janot
reflections.text:
This people-centred normative learning response might in the USA trigger the tiresome nanny state debate around “me responsible for me” so public investment should minimise "me responsible for we” spending. Brother’s keeper aside, the contrast is telling. Some years ago, Pablo & I were working on an urban development game for the Nordic Climate Festival (with Mohini Dutta & Ben Norskov, called Broken Cities:). Playtesting the game with Federico, a friend from Equatorial Guinea, I was surprised that he consistently chose to invest in the cheaper very climate unfriendly options - & was further surprised by his surprise that we didn’t see the obvious answer: people need housing. I was to be surprised Again when we played the game in Finland at the festival w/a large cohort of nordic university students. They consistently played to optimise clean green development. It struck me that during playtesting, urban planning students from many ethnic & economic backgrounds in Boston did Not have such a unified sense of social contract - green or otherwise. Debriefing w/the nordic students, I shared Federico’s strategy & rationale. As it turned out, the best learning outcome of the game was the realisation that while equally committed to upholding an equitable social contract, the divergence in strategies illuminated how prioritising basic human needs is intrinsic to - and needs to be explicit in - climate-responsive development. 
Best, Janot

title: Future Library
summary: Future Library is a 100-year artwork by Katie Paterson that began in 2014 with the planting of a forest in Nordmarka, near Oslo. Each year, one writer contributes a new manuscript that is sealed away unread and unpublished. In 2114, the trees from the forest will be harvested to make the paper on which all 100 manuscripts will finally be printed. The writers already include Margaret Atwood, David Mitchell, Han Kang, Ocean Vuong and Tsitsi Dangarembga, with the project deliberately asking both authors and institutions to commit to readers they will never meet.
thoughts: I like the idea of creating a tradition, and it is an opportunity to experience what it feels like for someone to create something that is only for our ancestors. If we plant a tree we at least get to see it grow, but the idea of locking something away that we can't use / enjoy ourselves feels quite frustrating! I'm guessing there are parallels with funding and designing climate adaptation and risk reduction measures - should we think about designing-in co-benefits for current generations?
image_credit: Photograph: Alequihdez · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
discovery: Future Library is an unusually literal act of trust in the future. The writers surrender control over when, how and by whom their work will be read, while the project itself depends on institutions and communities maintaining a promise for a century. It makes long-term thinking feel less like prediction and more like stewardship: creating something valuable now while accepting that its meaning may only become clear to people we will never know.

reflections.name: Janot
reflections.text:
EEK I am stunned that the plan is to harvest the trees in 100 yrs to make PAPER - by then please oh please let us be making paper from sargassum or some sustainably circular source!!
Maybe the unsealing & publishing of the manuscripts could instead inspire Daily Hummingbird responses;) That said, the Future Library project reminds me of a recent visit to Angers to see the approx 600-yr old Apocalypse tapestry...and the serendipitous surprise of arriving just in time to also see a new series of tapestries - all done using classical Aubusson methods - depicting the Tolkien illustrations from Lord of the Rings in splendrous grandeur of scale and colour!
:) Janot

reflections.name: Macarena
reflections.text:
There’s undeniable beauty in the Future Library’s commitment to hope and
long-term thinking, but I find it quite disconnected from the urgent
realities of climate change. It feels almost arrogant that, in 2014, when
we were already aware of accelerating climate disruption, we assumed we
could simply preserve a forest for 100 years. We continue to act as though
we can control nature while ignoring how rapidly it is degrading, and
dissapearing, largely because the way we carry our lives, business and
economies. Will that forest even exist in 2114? Or will the Future Library
become a beautiful reminder of how much effort we put into preserving
stories for the future, while failing to take the action needed to ensure
we actually have one?

title: The Fish Doorbell
summary: Every spring, thousands of fish migrate through Utrecht’s canals towards spawning grounds, but their route is interrupted by the historic Weerdsluis lock. In 2021, the city introduced the world’s first “Fish Doorbell”: an underwater livestream lets anyone watching online press a digital bell when fish are gathering at the closed lock. The signal goes to the lock keeper, who can then open the gates when enough fish are waiting. In its first season alone, people rang the bell more than 100,000 times; the project has since become an annual fixture attracting viewers from around the world.
thoughts: I already knew about this, and had rung the doorbell! The fish doorbell is such a catchy, silly name and even if there isn't evidence that this has improved fish ecology, what a fantastic example of the reach of these kinds of citizen science initiatives. It made me wonder if we could use this kind of idea as a locally-led trigger for anticipatory action, for example people could 'ring the doorbell' when their indigenous forecast techniques are telling them a flood is coming.
image_credit: Photograph: Japiot · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
discovery: The Fish Doorbell turns a hidden ecological process into something people can notice, understand and help with. Its charm matters: a small, playful interface makes participation feel immediate rather than abstract. It is a reminder that good design can create a relationship with a problem before it asks people to care about solving it.

reflections.name: Janot
reflections.text:
The crowd-sourced data from observers ringing the fish doorbell is a great 
example of a human system (canal & locks) taking corrective responsibility 
for interrupting natural systems (access to spawning grounds) but it also 
illustrates the utility in trusting crowd-sourced data for early warning 
systems. In Togo when the national weather service could not afford to 
maintain rainfall guage @ river level readings, over 1500 Red Cross 
volunteers were trained as observers to SMS daily readings directly into a 
data base, which in turn fed a Red Cross machine learning flood prediction 
model used by communities to prepare for high water…but the government 
agencies who trained the observers do not use the data because it is not 
validated. Here at the dawn of the big data era it’s great to see the 
Weerdsluis lock using trusted crowd-sourced data!

reflections.name: Erin
reflections.text:
This is so sweet. I sent it to a bunch of friends and family, which made
them all happy. It is lovely to share a story about people coming together
about something so sweet. What I find most interesting about the story is
the naming of the webcam a "doorbell". I think that humanization of the
process is probably what attracted so much attention, and it reminds me how
important it is to incorporate imagination and whimsy when you want to
start a movement.

reflections.name: Macarena
reflections.text:
I want to believe there is a genuine interest in coming closer to nature,
curiosity... but, I also see that this seamlessly harmless experiment
represents how over and over, we think we can control nature,  that we are
to control nature,  and that ultimately, this is just another way of
greenwashing. The empty or just unjustified management of natural resources
behind the "I am improving nature" kind of message.

title: One Million Checkboxes
summary: In June 2024, developer Nolen Royalty launched One Million Checkboxes: a webpage containing one million shared checkboxes, where every tick or untick was immediately visible to everyone else. He expected a few hundred users; instead, more than half a million people visited and collectively changed boxes more than 650 million times before the site was closed two weeks later. Players quickly moved beyond random clicking, using scripts and coordinated activity to create patterns, images and even hidden messages across the shared grid.
thoughts: I think this shows how when we create something it can take on a beautiful life of its own that we perhaps couldn't have ever predicted. And I love how a group of strangers found a way to connect with the original developer.
image_credit: Nolen Royalty (Itseieio) · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
discovery: One Million Checkboxes is a reminder that participation is rarely predictable from the structure we design for it. A deliberately pointless interface became a space for play, coordination, competition and collective invention because people brought their own purposes to it. Sometimes the most interesting behaviour in a system is not what its designer intended, but what emerges once many people begin interacting through it.

reflections.name: Macarena
reflections.text:
We always seem to organize ourselves, we simply can’t help it. Whether
driven by competition with others or ourselves, or a desire to share what
wecare caosble of, we naturally seek structure and a sense of belonging
within a group, leading to aligning with the collective whole, or at least
most of us do!

reflections.name: Janot
reflections.text:
William “Smitty” Smith, late founder of the National Center for Race Amity 
(Atlanta) once remarked to me that we really do not have a science of the 
human being. The I mil checkboxes Hummingbird reminds me of something that 
emerged from handling population datasculptures for dozens of countries. 
This was Pablo Suarez’s inspiration - late great climate, math & Caring 
geek! We created 3D printed population datasculptures, as an invitation to 
interrogate country data over the last 50 years or so, that presented as 
tables on a page or spreadsheet would be too boring to whip up a frenzy of 
interest. And which the datasculptures unfailingly do. At first we started 
noticing the obvious mega trends - a world war is almost indistinguishable 
from a pandemic, dramatic differences in same age male & female numbers 
highlight gender inequities at a glance & generally point to regional 
cultural drivers, however the most subtle - and perhaps most provocative of 
further investigation - is the across the board - All countries - increase 
in lifespan combined with a contraction in birth rates. Human population 
data from the past 50 years completely debunks the 1960s/70s “Population 
Bomb” theory. The classic population pyramid profile is inexorably becoming 
a population pear. There appear to be self-limiting mechanisms operating as 
a sort of hidden hive consciousness - which we scarcely recognize, let 
alone understand. What emerged from the One Million Checkboxes also 
reflects an extraordinary but surprisingly ordinary (in that we all have it 
- whatever *it* is - to hand) self-organizing capacity for co-creative 
ideation. We may collectively, as a species, be “the problem”. Human nature 
may be far less self-sustaining and vastly more hive-sustaining than we 
have yet to imagine.
Onwards!

reflections.name: Erin
reflections.text:
Ok why did all the users not crash the site?? But thinking bigger, how do
you predict what will go viral at any given time?

title: Ise Jingu
summary:
At Ise Jingu in Japan, the main Shinto shrine buildings are completely rebuilt every 20 years in a tradition known as Shikinen Sengu. The practice dates back more than 1,300 years and requires each generation of craftspeople to recreate the buildings, furnishings and ritual objects using traditional methods. Rather than preserving the same physical structure indefinitely, the process preserves the knowledge, skills and practices needed to rebuild it.

Kyodo News illustrated feature on the current rebuilding cycle: https://immersive.kyodonews.net/ise-jingu/index.html
thoughts: We've been thinking a lot about disaster memory recently, and I generally think of memorials to floods which are in some ways designed to make sure people don't forget. However, this is a much more active way of engaging with history, and I wonder how to apply it to disasters.
image_credit: Photograph: Zairon · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
discovery: Ise Jingu offers a striking alternative to the idea that resilience means making something last forever. The buildings are temporary, but the capability to recreate them is deliberately renewed across generations. It suggests that continuity can depend less on preserving an object unchanged than on repeatedly practising the knowledge, relationships and skills needed to rebuild it.

reflections.name: Erin
reflections.text:
What parts of our lives do we struggle to rebuild when they break? What
would it look like to practice that rebuilding before things break? In a
way that is celebratory rather than scared?

reflections.name: Macarena
reflections.text:
At a time when long-term perspectives and enduring, resilient, approaches
to living, particularly regarding buildings and places, are top of mind for
me, this story leaves me feeling quite divided. And it makes me wonder how
this tradition could be about enhancing places, instead of tearing them
down, passing this tradition also far beyond their immediate physical as
well as time boundaries. But I am no one to change traditions!

title: Dear Data
summary: Dear Data was a year-long project by information designers Giorgia Lupi and Stefanie Posavec. Each week, while living on opposite sides of the Atlantic, they chose one aspect of their everyday lives to track — from clocks and purchases to smiles, indecision and physical contact — then turned the data into a hand-drawn postcard and mailed it to the other person. Across 52 weeks, the project became both a record of their lives and a friendship built through data, using visualisation not just to quantify behaviour but to notice and communicate experience.
thoughts: Such a creative experiment! On one hand, what a burden to be constantly recording data on the most seemingly mundane things. But also a reminder that in general we don't capture 'data' on some of the most beautiful things, like laughter, compliments and hugs. Then also behind this is a committed friendship and an example of how a single brief can result in two often very different outcomes. I didn't realise, but this probably inspired Hummingbird (this was a pre-website Inspiration that I decided to include)
image_credit: Photograph: Sara Di Franco · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
discovery: Dear Data shows that data can be a way of paying attention, not just measuring performance. By choosing what to notice and then drawing it by hand, the project turns everyday experience into something reflective and relational. It suggests that the value of data sometimes lies less in precision than in the questions it encourages us to ask about our own lives and about one another.

reflections.name: Macarena
reflections.text:
I’m quite struck by how much care for the other person and human connection
this experiment/ story shows. The data points themselves, collected day by
day, might not tell us much about someone on their own. But collecting
them, bringing them together in a drawing, and posting them! to someone
else with tireless effort, that’s care, that’s dedication! Imagine if we
all approached our lives (and datashsring) and communication with this
level of care and intention. How much better could we be at joining the
dots, seeing the bigger picture and creating meaningful impact?

title: The Thing From The Future
summary: The Thing From The Future is an imagination game created by Stuart Candy and Jeff Watson in which players combine cards describing a type of future, a domain, an object and a mood, then invent an artefact that could plausibly exist in that world. The print-and-play deck contains more than 3.7 million possible prompt combinations, deliberately forcing players away from a single expected future and towards multiple, sometimes uncomfortable or surprising possibilities. The game has subsequently been adapted for workshops, education and digital play.
thoughts: This was an older inspiration that I've recycled for the website. I've used the online version a number of times to help get people into an imaginative frame of mind within meetings. It's interesting to see the differences in the 'objects' that people imagine from the same prompts, sometimes revealing something previously unknown about their personalities!
image_credit: Stuart Candy and Jeff Watson · The Thing From The Future (Print-and-Play Edition), 2015 · CC BY-NC-SA
discovery: Most planning starts by asking what is likely to happen. The Thing From The Future asks a different question: what could exist if the surrounding world changed enough? That shift matters because imagination is not the opposite of rigour; it can be a way of exposing assumptions that ordinary planning leaves untouched. A strange imagined object can make an unfamiliar future concrete enough to discuss, challenge and design for.

title: What people actually do in an emergency
summary: In 2017, an accidental explosion and small fire on a London Underground train was captured on CCTV, allowing researchers to analyse the immediate reactions of 40 passengers. Rather than a uniform response of panic and flight, they observed remarkably varied behaviours. Some passengers ran, others walked, six initially retrieved belongings, five stopped to observe what was happening, and five waited or moved aside to let others pass. Researchers identified only two instances of antisocial behaviour, alongside numerous examples of cooperation, including passengers making space for others and a parent shielding her child. The study provides unusually detailed evidence of how people behave during a real, unexpected emergency.
thoughts: The research itself points to how initial reactions to an explosion show a high degree of variability, but over time behaviour becomes more homogenous. I think this is worth considering when thinking about early warning systems and anticipating unprecedented extremes, particularly for rapid onset hazards. How do people respond to an early warning, and how do interactions with others shape that response? And if we can understand that better, how might we design early warning systems differently to account for that?
image_credit: Photograph: Dr Neil Clifton · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
discovery: Disaster systems can be remarkably paternalistic, often assuming that people will panic, misunderstand uncertainty or need tightly controlled instructions. Yet real emergencies frequently show something more complex: people retain judgement, relationships and a capacity to help one another. Perhaps warning systems should leave more room for people themselves to cope intelligently when the prescribed response does not quite fit. A system designed around compliance may look very different from one designed around enabling judgement.

title: The Evolution of Trust
summary:
The Evolution of Trust is an interactive browser game by Nicky Case that uses repeated game-theory scenarios to explore how cooperation, mistrust, retaliation and forgiveness emerge between individuals. Players test different strategies against one another and can alter conditions such as the frequency of mistakes or the likelihood of meeting again, showing how small changes in the rules of interaction can produce very different collective outcomes.

Background on the game and its game-theory foundations: https://exploring-economics.org/en/discover/the-evolution-of-trust/
thoughts: Pablo Suarez used to say that “change happens at the speed of trust”. I like that this is an interactive game which speaks to that, using game theory (the prisoner's dilemma) to support a message of "Build relationships. Find win-wins. Communicate clearly"
discovery: The game shows that trust is not simply a virtue; it can be a practical condition for successful cooperation. In repeated versions of the Prisoner’s Dilemma, the best collective outcomes emerge when people expect to interact again, can communicate, find mutually beneficial arrangements, and have enough forgiveness to recover from occasional mistakes. “Build relationships. Find win-wins. Communicate clearly” is therefore not just good interpersonal advice: game theory helps explain why these behaviours can make cooperation more resilient.

title: The Wind Phone
summary: In a garden in Japan, an unconnected telephone allows people to speak to loved ones they have lost. What began as one person's response to grief has become a place of comfort for thousands of visitors.
thoughts: After the Nepal floods I started to reflect more on how a fatality shouldn't be just a statistic. This is a powerful reminder that for every death there are many people grieving that death, and that grief is carried through time. Creating gentle ways for people to grieve should be an important part of disaster response, and not just in the immediate aftermath.
image_credit: Photograph: Matthew Komatsu · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
discovery: The Wind Phone demonstrates how a simple idea can transform how we understand loss. It reminds us that the consequences of a death extend far beyond the individual.
